overview: Heston (1993) grants volatility what Black–Scholes denied it: a life of its own. Variance follows its own mean-reverting square-root process, correlated with the stock — and that correlation is the smile's engine. With ρ < 0, crashes and volatility spikes arrive together, fattening the left tail exactly where equity markets fear it, so out-of-the-money puts price rich relative to lognormal — which is what the observed skew *is*. The model's enduring appeal: all this while keeping a semi-closed form, two probabilities recovered by integrating a characteristic function.
formula_latex: dS = (r - q) S\,dt + \sqrt{v}\,S\,dW_S, \quad dv = \kappa(\theta - v)\,dt + \xi\sqrt{v}\,dW_v, \quad dW_S dW_v = \rho\,dt

variables.name: Initial variance
variables.why_it_matters: Today's instantaneous variance — set here from your volatility input as σ². It anchors the short-dated ATM level of the smile.

variables.name: Mean-reversion speed
variables.why_it_matters: How fast variance returns to θ. High κ makes vol shocks transient — flattening the long end of the vol term structure.

variables.name: Vol-of-vol
variables.why_it_matters: The randomness of volatility itself: the curvature knob. ξ = 0 collapses the model to Black–Scholes (the test suite enforces this); large ξ bends the smile's wings upward.

variables.name: Spot/vol correlation
variables.why_it_matters: The skew knob. Negative ρ (equities live near −0.7) ties falling prices to rising vol — the leverage effect — tilting implied vols against low strikes.

assumptions: Variance follows a square-root (CIR-type) process: mean-reverting, non-negative given the Feller condition 2κθ ≥ ξ².
One volatility factor with constant κ, θ, ξ, ρ over the option's life.
Continuous paths — no jumps in either the stock or its variance.
limitations: Short-dated smiles are too flat: diffusive vol cannot build enough skew in a week — that job needs jumps.
Calibration is an art: several parameter sets can fit today's smile while implying different dynamics (and different exotic prices).
When the Feller condition fails — as fitted parameters often make it — variance touches zero and simulation requires care.
One vol factor cannot decouple the smile's level from its term structure; markets sometimes move them independently.
when_to_use: Pricing and hedging with smile consistency across strikes and maturities; forward-starting options and cliquets where vol dynamics (not just today's smile) matter; as the standard stochastic-vol benchmark.
when_not_to_use: Very short-dated skew (jump models or SVJ), products needing exact fit to every quoted vol (local vol interpolates better), or wherever a vanilla-only book makes Black–Scholes-plus-smile sufficient.
industry_usage: A workhorse of equity and FX exotics desks, usually with jumps bolted on (Bates) or embedded in local-stochastic-vol hybrids; the reference model stochastic-vol papers measure themselves against.
computational_complexity: Semi-closed form: two numerical integrals of a complex characteristic function — milliseconds here (4,000-point quadrature, the numerically stable 'little trap' formulation).
comparison_note: Against Black–Scholes at the same input vol, Heston's ATM price lands close while its wings differ: negative correlation shifts value toward low-strike puts and away from the lognormal's symmetric optimism. The gap you see is the price of acknowledging that volatility moves — and moves *with* the market.
